question.prompt: Consider the sequence of numbers \(4,\) \(7,\) \(1,\) \(8,\) \(9,\) \(7,\) \(6,\) \(\ldots\) For \(n \gt 2,\) the \(n\)th term of the sequence is the units digit of the sum of the two previous terms. Let \(S_n\) denote the sum of the first \(n\) terms of this sequence. The smallest value of \(n\) for which \(S_n \gt 10{,}000\) is

solutions.explanation:
Because each new term depends on the previous two terms, look for a repeated consecutive pair. Repeating a single term would not be enough to determine what follows.

Continuing the units-digit rule gives the first twelve terms
\[
4,7,1,8,9,7,6,3,9,2,1,3.
\]
The next two terms are \(4\) and \(7\), since \(1+3=4\) and \(3+4=7\). Thus terms \(13,14\) repeat the starting pair. The same pair always produces the same next term, so the entire twelve-term block repeats indefinitely.

One block sums to \(60\). Therefore \(166\) complete blocks contain \(166\cdot12=1992\) terms and have sum
\[
S_{1992}=166\cdot60=9960.
\]
The next block must contribute more than \(40\) to cross the threshold. Its first six terms sum to
\[
4+7+1+8+9+7=36,
\]
and its seventh term is \(6\). Hence
\[
S_{1998}=9996,
\qquad
S_{1999}=10002.
\]
All terms are nonnegative, so every earlier partial sum is at most \(S_{1998}\). The smallest required index is therefore \(\boxed{1999}\), choice B.
solutions.title: Prove a repeating block and add whole blocks
